doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Favourite instrument and playing tenor against Scott Hamilton and Harry Allen
summary: He has no favourite horn, chooses by the band, and talks about his hot tenor style compared with Scott Hamilton, Harry Allen and Scott Robinson.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well you definitely have some musical genes in your blood. I mean, being at this festival, the first night I heard you playing the trumpet. Last night and let’s see this afternoon I heard you playing tenor sax. Later on in the day I heard you playing alto sax. And you seem to wail on all of them. Do you have a favorite?

It all depends on the mood, and what kind of band it is. Really it’s — that kind of band like the last one where I was playing alto, I wouldn’t have wanted to play anything but alto. Because there was already a four-piece front line — there was trumpet, clarinet, trombone and tenor. So for me to double on any of those would have been not as fun as playing the alto. And trying to fit in, trying to play something that didn’t get in their way. Because a five-piece front line is very difficult. But some bands you know you have to play the trumpet, other bands I want to play the clarinet, trombone’s my newest one. I’m not there yet, but I’m working hard on it. But it just depends on the band and the mood.
When I heard you play tenor, it was interesting because you were four of you together. And in my ears, you were the most aggressive player there. Do you agree with that?
I mean you had Scott Hamilton and a couple of other guys who are mainstreamish players I guess — I don’t know, labels are tough. But I almost could hear you playing in a rhythm & blues band too.

Um hum. I probably get, if I got hot at all I get hot probably sooner, because I’m not used to playing — like Scott can play, he can go up in a very gradual incline and get hotter and hotter and hotter and hotter. And at the end of it, wow. I can’t do that. I dive in with both feet and then I really can only play two or three choruses and then I run out of ideas. I need to do it more or something, or listen to Scott. But Harry Allen’s great. He can start slow and then expand, and then you think he’s going to stop and then he expands a bit more. And Scott Robinson, I’d never met Scott before. I’d never met Harry either. I’ve heard them on records but I’ve never met Scott. And he plays amazing eclectic things.

You know, up high and down low. Perfect command of all the instruments, and he stands with a deadpan look — what’s he going to do now? It’s a lovely tone. He’s completely in command of what he’s doing. And he doesn’t sound like anyone else either.
